questions.question: Which fields does one JSONL Example carry in this harness?
options: id, prompt, targets, metric, plus optional extras for metric-specific data such as io_pairs.
task_name, model_weights, and one scalar score produced before generation.
Only a prompt and one target string; metrics are selected by the filename.
id, prompt, and a precomputed latency; the adapter never sees targets.
questions.explanation: load_task_jsonl builds Example from those fields. targets support multiple references, while extras carries side inputs needed by code_exec.

questions.question: Why does a metric function receive (prediction, targets, extras)?
options: It lets the metric mutate the model before scoring each example.
It supports one or more reference strings and optional side data while returning a comparable scalar score.
It is required only because JSON cannot represent floats.
It makes every metric return an integer count rather than a score.
questions.explanation: Exact match and multiple choice use targets; ROUGE-L can choose the best reference; code_exec reads extras['io_pairs']. The runner treats each result as a float.

questions.question: What boundary does metric_code_exec enforce around a submitted function?
options: It runs the code in a Docker container with a kernel-enforced CPU quota.
It accepts only one-line lambdas and rejects every def statement.
It executes in a stripped builtins namespace exposing a small allowlist; imports and filesystem/network access are not available through that namespace.
It compares the source text with a stored reference without executing it.
questions.explanation: The function uses exec with a restricted __builtins__ dictionary, then calls a local function named f on each io_pairs input. This is a narrow lesson harness, not a full OS sandbox.

questions.question: What boundary does the ModelAdapter protocol provide?
options: It performs the statistical significance test after the leaderboard is written.
It owns the tokenizer vocabulary and therefore removes the need for task prompts.
It stores task JSONL and decides which metric each example uses.
It is the replaceable generate(prompts) -> list[str] boundary; tasks, metrics, and leaderboard aggregation stay unchanged when the model backend changes.
questions.explanation: ToyAdapter implements the same generate and name surface a real adapter would use. The runner does not need to know how outputs were produced.

questions.question: Why does Leaderboard write the schema string leaderboard.v1?
options: A reader can dispatch or migrate when the JSON shape changes instead of silently treating a newer file as the old format.
It lets the adapter skip generation when two runs have the same schema.
It compresses each task result into a smaller JSON token.
It orders tasks alphabetically without inspecting their names.
questions.explanation: The schema is explicit metadata for consumers of the artifact. Versioning the shape is separate from the score and from task ordering.

questions.question: How is overall_score computed by run_leaderboard?
options: It is the sum of all correct examples, so larger task suites dominate.
It is the mean of the task-level scores; inspect per-example records as well because one aggregate can hide a regression in a specific task.
It is the maximum task score, which rewards the strongest capability.
It is the mean latency of the adapter, independent of metric values.
questions.explanation: The code computes sum(r.score for r in results) / len(results), giving each task equal weight regardless of its example count. The optional per-example output preserves the evidence behind that mean.
